Dear Dr Smith,

Re: 	Mr John Smith. DOB 12/12/1970

I reviewed this 45-year-old man in clinic today, together with his wife. He was referred for ongoing management of his epilepsy and so I will recap his epilepsy history.

Mr Smith was born normally. He had one febrile seizure at the age of 3 years. He had a mild viral meningitis at the age of 18 years but has not had any encephalitis or significant head injuries.  He had three A-levels and studied law at university before going on to work as a solicitor. At the age of 32 he had a significant collapse and was found to have a sub-arachnoid haemorrhage due to a ruptured ACA aneurysm. This was treated with endovascular coiling. He possibly had one seizure at the time of the subarachnoid haemorrhage but was not started on medication as it was thought that this was an acute symptomatic seizures.

Three years later, at the age of 35 he had two episodes of transient loss of consciousness which were thought to be tonic-clonic seizures and he was diagnosed with epilepsy at the age of 36. Initially he was treated with phenytoin but this was switched to levetiracetam 2 years ago. Currently he is taking 750mg twice a day of the levetiracetam and his last seizure was 2 years ago. He has returned to work and is driving. He lives with his wife and two daughters. His eldest daughter had 2 febrile seizures and had childhood absence epilepsy although she is now seizure free. He doesn’t smoke but drinks around 12 units of alcohol (6 cans of lager) a week.

Apart from the epilepsy he takes ramipril for hypertension and simvastatin for hypercolestrolaemia.

Mr Smith does find that he is very irritable and short tempered since starting the levetiracetam. This seems to be having an effect on his quality of life and he would be very keen to change this.

His neurological examination today was essentially normal. Blood pressure was 126/67, his pulse was 68 and regular.

A recent CT scan on 3/7/2016 is degraded but the artefact from the coil but does show an area of gliosis in the right frontal lobe. An EEG from 1990 shows slow waves with ocassional right sided sharp waves.
